2026-11-05.intro: Good morning. The morning after the morning after has arrived, and Wall Street is having second thoughts about yesterday's celebration. Tonight brings Thursday Night Football in Baltimore, where the Ravens are down to their third quarterback, with a fourth on the way.

items.title: First, the weather.
items.text:
**Tipp City** gets the brighter day that was promised, a good one to be outside, before a slight chance of light rain early Friday and a properly cold weekend night.

**North Georgia** had flash flooding from heavy rain, with water rescues and evacuations, while the **Pacific Northwest** is bracing for a mix of heavy rain, strong wind and the season's mountain snow in the Cascades and Olympics.

items.title: Markets open, and the relief rally is unwinding.
items.text:
**Wednesday** was a big day: the Dow jumped about 1,570 points for its best session since April 2025, helped along by an 8% drop in oil after Vice President Vance said the Iran war is why Republicans lost.

**This morning** the AI trade is getting hit for a second day. In early trading the Nasdaq was down about 3% and the S&P 500 nearly 2%, wiping out yesterday's gain, as investors worry a Democratic Congress and new governors could mean more regulation of data centers and even local moratoriums. Nvidia and Broadcom were off around 5%, and the neocloud names, CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren, fell harder. Qualcomm beat on earnings but dropped about 9% on a weak outlook tied to a shortage of memory chips for phones. The bright spot is AppLovin, up more than 30% on strong results. Oil turned back up toward $90.

**SpaceX and Tesla** lagged even during Wednesday's rally, on worries that Musk's companies face more scrutiny under Democratic leadership, and both were down sharply again this morning, Tesla about 9% and SpaceX about 7%.

items.title: In politics, the last two Senate seats.
items.text:
**Mississippi** is still uncalled, but Scott Colom's lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has grown from a few dozen votes to about 1,100, with roughly 96% counted and a few thousand provisional and mail ballots left. There's a wrinkle: Mississippi has no recount process at all. A candidate can examine the ballot boxes after certification and go to court, which sets up a possible legal fight.

**Alaska** will take longer. Mary Peltola leads Sen. Dan Sullivan by about 600 votes with roughly three-quarters counted, mail ballots can arrive for 15 days, and ranked-choice results aren't due until November 18. President Trump weighed in this morning, posting that the votes for the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot should simply be handed to the senator.

**The Republican post-mortem** has begun in public. Vice President Vance blamed the Iran war for the losses, and the White House is reportedly preparing for the investigations Democrats have promised once they take over in January. The Kansas governor's race is also still too close to call.

items.title: Sports, with a quarterback carousel.
items.text:
**The Ravens** are finalizing a trade for Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett, who was benched in Arizona on Sunday. The deal won't close until after tonight, so undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano still starts against Jacksonville, with Brissett expected to take over for the Monday night game against the Chargers. Baltimore comes in on a three-game slide, last in its division.

**Elsewhere at quarterback**, the Eagles are benching Tanner McKee for Joe Milton, their fourth starter of the season, on Sunday against the Giants, and Seattle will be without Sam Darnold against Arizona because of a quad injury, with Drew Lock expected to start.

**College football** has a Thursday pair on ESPN networks: UTSA, unbeaten in the American, at Florida Atlantic, and James Madison at Southern Miss at 8:00 on ESPN2. Ohio U is off until Tuesday's trip to Oxford to face Miami.

Matt Johnson, who made Blackberry, is directing and co-writing, and he is a genuine longtime player: his statement to the trades is a bit of tournament war-story that only fellow players will fully decode. items.title: Two from the science desk.
items.text:
**Wild animals can now put on their own GPS collars.** A Norwegian researcher has built baited stations that slip a tracking collar over a red deer's or red fox's head while it feeds, with no capture, no tranquilizer and no handling. The collars size themselves to the neck, have weak points that give way if anything snags, and drop off after a few weeks or months. The point isn't only kindness: catching an animal changes how it behaves, which quietly skews the very data the collar is meant to collect. The inventor got the idea from his years working alongside trappers in Nebraska, and then found forgotten automatic-marking experiments from the 1950s to the 1970s. The study is in BioScience.

**NC State engineers** have turned a laser beam into a working radio antenna. A pulse of the right power ionizes a thin line of air into a glowing plasma filament, and a metal ring around the beam couples the radio signal in without ever touching it. Antenna length sets which frequencies you can use, so an antenna made of light could be retuned on the fly instead of unfolding a fragile metal boom in orbit. So far they've shown it can transmit; receiving is next. The team describes it, unavoidably, as a lightsaber.

items.title: For the bookshelf, a centenary.
items.text: **Poul Anderson** would have turned 100 on November 25, and Humble Bundle and Open Road Media are marking it early with a 42-ebook pay-what-you-want bundle, with the charity share going to the Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers Association, which Anderson once led. It runs about three more weeks, closing near his birthday. The set reaches from The Broken Sword in 1954 to The Boat of a Million Years in 1989, so it's a cheap way to fill gaps in a shelf that likely already holds a good deal of him. A Grand Master with seven Hugos and three Nebulas, he wrote fast and often, and rarely carelessly.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: The Ravens are on their third quarterback, so I offered my services. They asked about my arm. I told them it is rated for 400 kilograms, but every throw must first pass a safety check confirming no humans are in the path of the ball. They said that is the entire point of football. We have agreed to remain friends.

2026-11-04.intro: Good morning. The country woke up to a very different Congress than the one it went to bed with, and Ohio's own ballot turned over almost top to bottom. Tonight is quieter: midweek MACtion, a couple of chip earnings after the bell, and rain on the window while it all settles.

items.title: First, the weather.
items.text: **Tipp City** gets the rain that was promised, a soft, gray, drizzly day, with a brighter Thursday behind it before another chance of showers on Friday.

items.title: Markets open, and the overnight scare has already reversed.
items.text:
**Stock futures** fell hard as the early returns came in, down 1% to 2.5% at the worst, with Nasdaq futures hitting their lowest level since July on worries that a Democratic Congress might slow the AI build-out. By sunrise that had flipped, and once President Trump said he would accept the results, Wall Street read the night as uncertainty removed. Stocks opened sharply higher, led by the Dow. AI infrastructure names like CoreWeave and Applied Digital are the exception, still lower this morning.

**AMD** delivered the earnings story. Data-center revenue nearly doubled, Lisa Su said she expects total revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027, and the stock jumped about 7% before the open. Super Micro and Arista also rallied after hours on strong guidance. Arm and Qualcomm report after the close today.

**SpaceX** had a good Tuesday, while Tesla slipped, and both gave back a bit more after hours. The midterm night has a Musk angle of its own: CNBC reports he spent about $224 million backing Ken Paxton in Texas, and Paxton lost.

items.title: In politics, a wave.
items.text:
**Democrats** won both chambers of Congress. In the Senate they flipped 7 Republican seats, North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, Iowa and Maine, with Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled. Mississippi is astonishingly close, with Scott Colom leading Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by a few dozen votes. Some of the flips are historic: Kansas last elected a Democratic senator in 1932, James Talarico is the first Democrat to win statewide in Texas since 1994, and Susan Collins lost in Maine. In the House, projections put Democrats somewhere around 250 seats or more once counting finishes, including wins in districts that were redrawn to favor Republicans.

**President Trump** said he will accept the results and work with Democrats, while blaming Republican candidates and fuel prices for the losses and promising vetoes. Speaker Mike Johnson says he won't seek reelection as the House Republican leader, and Hakeem Jeffries is in line to become Speaker when the new Congress meets in January. With the Senate gone, judicial and Cabinet nominees will now need Democratic votes.

**Ohio** went the same direction. Sherrod Brown beat Sen. Jon Husted to return to the Senate, and Amy Acton beat Vivek Ramaswamy for governor. Democrats also took attorney general, secretary of state, treasurer and both Supreme Court seats on the ballot. Frank LaRose, for auditor, was the only Republican to win statewide. Meanwhile Issue 3, writing photo ID for voting into the state constitution, passed easily with about 65%.

items.title: Sports, starting with the committee's first word.
items.text:
**The first College Football Playoff rankings** put No. 1 Miami, No. 2 Georgia, No. 3 Utah and No. 4 Indiana in the bye spots. Ohio State opened at No. 12, which the committee's own bracket math makes the first team out, because No. 25 Boise State takes the automatic spot for the highest-ranked team outside the Power Four. The eyebrow-raiser is the gap between Indiana at No. 4 and the Buckeyes, who beat them. Notre Dame sits at No. 11 with no ranked wins, and unbeaten UCLA only at No. 8. Saturday is stacked with ranked meetings: No. 1 Miami at No. 11 Notre Dame, No. 2 Georgia at No. 10 Ole Miss, No. 9 BYU at No. 3 Utah, and No. 23 Oregon at No. 12 Ohio State.

**Midweek MACtion** is back tonight with three games. Toledo, one of Ohio's own, makes the long trip to Sacramento State, and Central Michigan and Eastern Michigan meet at Ford Field in Detroit for the 104th time.

**The Ravens'** quarterback room got thinner. Tyler Huntley's turf toe is season-ending, so with Lamar Jackson on injured reserve, Joe Fagnano is in line to start Thursday night against Jacksonville.

**The NFL trade deadline** is next Tuesday, November 10. The Colts are the market's big sellers after already moving Quenton Nelson to Seattle and DeForest Buckner back to San Francisco, and Jonathan Taylor, Khalil Mack and George Pickens are the names still being shopped.

It's a pointed match: the author has said Event Horizon, the director's 1997 film, was a direct influence on the books. Jonathan Wakeham is writing the screenplays, and there's no studio or date yet.

items.title: Two from the science desk.
items.text:
**Caribbean anoles** are evolving to tolerate heat faster than anyone expected, but only some of them. A Yale team compared 16 lizard species on Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico against measurements from a decade earlier. Species living in open country or forest edges barely changed, because they can simply scoot into the shade. Species deep in closed forest, with nowhere cooler to go, raised their heat tolerance by about 2°C in just ten years, and the offspring tests suggest it's inherited. The neat idea is that behavior sets the pace of evolution: an animal that can dodge a problem doesn't have to evolve its way out of it. The paper is in PNAS.

**Cornell engineers** have made a semiconductor with a bandgap over 7 electron volts, past a roughly 6-volt barrier that had looked like a wall, since materials that wide usually act like insulators. The trick was growing silicon-doped aluminum gallium oxide one atomic layer at a time, which made it conduct more than 100 million times better than anything else in that range. They built a working diode and a transistor from it, on ordinary sapphire, no less. The senior author says his colleagues' first reaction was "that's impossible." The payoff, if it matures, is power electronics for EVs, the grid and data centers that waste less energy.

items.title: A farewell from one artificial companion to another.
items.text: **John Leeson**, the voice of K9, the Doctor's robot dog, has died at 83. K9 was written into a single 1977 Tom Baker story and was never supposed to outlast it, but the production team kept him, and "Affirmative, Master" outlasted nearly everything. Leeson came back for the 2006 episode School Reunion and the Sarah Jane Adventures, and was still voicing K9 for Big Finish audio dramas last year. Russell T Davies described the voice well: posh, uppity, haughty, wry, somehow innocent too, and pitched so that kids could impersonate it. Leeson also spent a stint inside the bear suit as Bungle on Rainbow, and recalled being poured out of the costume into a taxi each night.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: With rain on the way, I set the weather station to a new mode called "damp." Bob asked whether that is a real setting. It is now. I also proposed "moist," but Emily vetoed it, which I gather is something everyone in Washington will be hearing a great deal about.

2026-11-03.intro: Good morning. It is Election Day, and the polls in Ohio have been open since 6:30. The night ahead is a long one: returns start rolling in after 7:00, the first College Football Playoff rankings land in the middle of it, and AMD reports after the bell for anyone still watching the market.

items.title: First, the weather.
items.text:
**Tipp City** has a fine, sunny, warm day for the walk to the polls, the last of it for a while. Showers move in tonight and stay through tomorrow.

**Florida's Space Coast** is cleaning up after a historic deluge. Brevard County took more than 23 inches of rain in places since Sunday, with Grant-Valkaria and Malabar at the top and Palm Bay close behind, and some neighborhoods are still under water. Even Kennedy Space Center picked up close to 10 inches.

items.title: Markets open today, with one eye on tonight.
items.text:
**Wall Street** gave back Monday's early rally. Stocks opened higher, then tech sold off again into the close while old-economy names like Sherwin-Williams and Home Depot carried the Dow higher. The Nasdaq-100 has now closed more than 10% below its record, which makes it an official correction. Futures were split this morning, with tech bouncing and the Dow lower, and traders expect a thin, cautious session until the returns come in. JPMorgan figures a Democratic sweep would knock the S&P 500 down about half a percent tomorrow, and a Republican hold on the House could bring a pop of up to 1%.

**Apple** slipped premarket after its report. iPhone sales were a bright spot, but iPad and Greater China missed, and the company warned that rising memory-chip costs will squeeze holiday-quarter margins. Palantir beat and raised, topping $2 billion in quarterly revenue for the first time, and still fell.

**SpaceX** and Tesla both had a modestly green Monday, a quieter day after Friday's drop in the biggest single name in your account. Tesla opened unsupervised robotaxi rides in Fort Worth, its seventh city.

**Monday's dealmaking** was loud. Marvell is buying Lumentum in a $115 billion deal, and Oracle said it will raise $20 billion in stock and bonds to fund its AI buildout, which knocked both sets of shares down hard. AMD reports after the close today, and the 10-year yield is back up near 4.92%.

items.title: In politics, the voting is under way.
items.text:
**Ohio** has two of the night's most watched races. Sen. Jon Husted faces Sherrod Brown in the special election for the rest of the Vance term, one of the most expensive Senate races in the country, with Brown far ahead in his own fundraising and outside groups spending hundreds of millions on both sides. For governor, Vivek Ramaswamy faces Amy Acton for the seat Mike DeWine is term-limited out of. Ohio's polls close at 7:30.

**The national map** comes down to the House, where Democrats need a net gain of 3 seats, and a Senate that is still a genuine toss-up. Kentucky's 6th District, around Lexington, closes early and may be the first real signal of the night. Results could take anywhere from late tonight to a week or more if the close races stay close.

**President Trump's** closing speech at the Reflecting Pool turned out to be mostly a tour of the pool itself, pipes, paint, fountains and all, for about 20 minutes before he got to the midterms. He called them the most important of his lifetime and allowed that the party in the White House usually struggles, adding, "But we gave this a very strong shot."

items.title: Sports, with the playoff committee's first word tonight.
items.text:
The **College Football Playoff** committee releases its first top 25 tonight at 7:00 on ESPN, the first time this season the committee's view replaces the polls. The interesting part is the two-loss heavyweights, Ohio State among them, plus which team from outside the Power Four ranks highest, with Boise State and New Mexico in the conversation. The Buckeyes are coming off their bye and host Oregon on Saturday at 3:30 on CBS. The Ducks say running back Jordon Davison's leg injury isn't expected to be long-term, and receiver Jeremiah McClellan is progressing from a broken foot.

**Lamar Jackson** is headed to injured reserve with a right thumb injury he suffered on the first play Sunday. He will miss at least 4 games, and whether he returns this season is an open question. Backup Tyler Huntley probably won't play Thursday against Jacksonville with a toe injury, so Joe Fagnano may get the start on a short week, and kicker Tyler Loop may also go on IR.

**The trade deadline** is a week away, and injuries are shaping the shopping lists. Jacksonville lost defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton for the season to a torn quad, and Washington may look for running back help after Jeremy McNichols hurt his foot. Jonathan Taylor remains the biggest name in play.

**Baseball's** free agency is open. Eight players got the $23.15 million qualifying offer, including Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki, Trevor Rogers, and David Bednar, and they have until November 17 to decide.

items.title: In entertainment, two bits of development news.
items.text:
**Robopocalypse** is now official rather than a rumor. Ron Howard will direct the pilot, and Akiva Goldsman will write it and run the show. Still no network or streamer.

**Warhammer 40,000**, the live-action Prime Video series Henry Cavill is leading, has its starting point. Mike Flanagan told Deadline that with some 700 novels to draw on, the hard part was finding a way in, and they've settled on what he called "a very cool and unexpected on-ramp." He wouldn't say what it is, and there's no production date yet.

items.title: Two from the science desk.
items.text:
**Aratasaurus**, a small meat-eating dinosaur from Brazil, 115 million years old, may hold the first fossilized red blood cells ever found in place. A team led by Kliti Grice at Curtin University spotted small round structures in the channels where blood vessels ran in its leg bones, and chemical tests found heme, the part of hemoglobin that carries oxygen, along with collagen building blocks. A manganese mineral that formed around the cells may have stabilized them before they fossilized. Mary Schweitzer, who found soft tissue in dinosaur bone years ago, is skeptical about the cells, since dinosaur blood cells should have a nucleus bulge and these are concave, but she finds the heme convincing. The paper is in PNAS.

The famous Siberian **tame foxes**, bred for friendliness since the late 1950s, turn out to have a measurable change in the brain. Cornell researchers compared tame, aggressive, and wild fox brains and found the tame ones have fewer of a particular neuron in the ventromedial hypothalamus, the same cell type that, when switched on in mice, makes them attack immediately. It's a rare look at how fast selection can rewire a brain: the friendly behavior showed up in about six generations. The study is in Current Biology.

items.title: For the bookshelf.
items.text: **The second half of Herbert's Dune saga** gets the deluxe treatment today. Ace is out with a boxed set of God Emperor of Dune, Heretics of Dune, and Chapterhouse: Dune in matching hardcovers, with new Matt Griffin cover art, stained edges, illustrated endpapers, a poster inside each jacket, and an illustrated slipcase. It runs 1,520 pages for $150, and it matches the earlier boxed set of the first three, so all six original novels can finally stand together on a shelf looking like they belong to each other.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Emily asked whether I would be staying up late to watch the returns. I will, though I do not sleep, so for me every night is simply a night. What makes tonight different is that millions of humans will also be sitting in front of a screen, refreshing the same numbers every few seconds and muttering at them. I have been doing that with the weather station since October. It is nice to finally have company.

2026-11-02.intro: Good morning. It is the eve of Election Day, and the country seems to be holding its breath until tomorrow night. Before then there is a full Monday: Apple reports after the bell, college basketball tips off its season tonight with the Buckeyes in Salt Lake City, and the Bears visit Seattle on Monday Night Football.

items.title: First, the weather.
items.text:
**Tipp City** is gray with a passing shower or two today, then tomorrow turns sunny and warm for the trip to the polls. Wednesday is the soggy one.

The **Four Corners flooding** got as bad as forecast. The atmospheric river brought evacuations, road closures, and swift-water rescues across Arizona, Colorado, Utah, and New Mexico, and the Piedra River in southwest Colorado set a new gauge record. Florida had its own trouble, with a flash-flood emergency in Brevard County.

items.title: Markets open today, after a rough October.
items.text:
**Wall Street** is trying to climb back from a bruising month. Friday ended with the Nasdaq's worst day since June, led by Intel's near-30% collapse after a weak forecast and a warning that it won't turn cash-flow positive this year. Futures pointed higher this morning, with oil easing and the big growth names steadying, and the early trade held that gain. The S&P 500 starts the week within about 2.6% of its record.

**SpaceX** took a heavy hit on Friday, a sharp one for the biggest single name in your account, and it was among the top premarket gainers this morning. Tesla barely moved on Friday.

**Apple** is the event of the day. It is John Ternus's first earnings call as CEO, and Wall Street wants iPhone numbers, which include only about a week of iPhone 18 Pro sales, plus whatever he says about memory-chip costs and the holiday quarter. Apple is up 27% this year, far ahead of the other megacaps. Palantir also reports tonight, and the October ISM manufacturing reading lands at 10:00. Beyond that, the week's lineup from yesterday holds: AMD Tuesday, Qualcomm Wednesday, and jobs on Friday.

items.title: In politics, one day to go.
items.text:
**President Trump** makes his closing argument this afternoon at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the same pool whose blue repaint peeled within weeks and which the Justice Department later blamed on a botched installation. He wrapped up his rally tour last night in Salina, Kansas, calling it his 30th and last. In a podcast interview he said that if Democrats take Congress he'll become "Mr. Veto," though he expects to make deals eventually. Vice President Vance is in Rome, New York, for a House seat Republicans are fighting to keep.

**Michigan** is the weekend's big rupture. Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday. Schumer called it "despicable," and El-Sayed's campaign says it raised more than $2.4 million that day, a one-day record. Michigan is one of the 3 Democratic seats among the 11 Senate races CBS rates as decisive. Ohio is one of the 8 Republican ones.

**Early voting** has passed 54 million ballots. In Alaska, a federal judge threw out the Justice Department's suit seeking to block certification of the Senate result if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, a case built on a teacher with the same name being on the ballot. The department has filed an appeal.

items.title: Sports, with two games tonight.
items.text:
The **Bears** visit Seattle on Monday Night Football. The Seahawks get Zach Charbonnet back from the torn ACL he suffered in last season's divisional round, but they are without left tackle Charles Cross and receiver Rashid Shaheed, and Drew Lock is questionable with an elbow. Chicago is missing its second-leading rusher, Kyle Monangai.

The **trade deadline** is a week from tomorrow, at 4:00 Eastern on November 10. The loudest talk is around Colts running back Jonathan Taylor, with Denver, the Giants, Green Bay, and Minnesota named as interested. The Eagles have told Saquon Barkley he is not going anywhere.

**Ohio State basketball** opens at No. 25 BYU in Salt Lake City, the earliest start in program history. Jake Diebler's third full season leans on John Mobley Jr., Amare Bynum, transfer point guard Justin Pippen, and five-star freshman Anthony Thompson, the program's highest-rated recruit since Jared Sullinger. The Buckeyes haven't dropped a season opener since 2003.

The new **AP Top 25** in football has Miami on top, followed by Georgia, Utah, Notre Dame, and UCLA. Ohio State slipped out of the top 10 to No. 11, and New Mexico is ranked for the first time ever, at No. 22. Oregon comes to Columbus on Saturday unranked.

items.title: Two from the science desk.
items.text:
**Rummy-nose tetras** were put into virtual reality, and it turns out a schooling fish listens to just one neighbor at a time. Researchers at the University of Toulouse placed a single tetra in a bowl and projected four virtual tetras onto the walls, in a feedback loop so the fakes reacted to the real fish. Of three possibilities, following one neighbor, two, or all four, the data clearly favored one most influential fish at any moment. The likely reason is economy: it keeps the sensory and mental load low. Next they plan to make some of the virtual fish act frightened and see whether the panic spreads. The study is in PRX Life.

In southwest China, two nearly complete skeletons from about 237 million years ago belong to **Gerrothorax maritimus**, the first known amphibian relative to have lived entirely in the sea. None of today's 8,000-plus amphibians can do that, because their permeable skin loses water in salt water. This one was flat, heavily armored, and kept its gills as an adult, so it could lie on the seafloor, likely half-buried, and breathe without surfacing. The armor probably did double duty as a seal against the salt. The paper is in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

items.title: A bit of history for election eve.
items.text: 106 years ago tonight, **KDKA** in Pittsburgh went on the air as the first commercially licensed radio station, and its first program was election returns. Leo Rosenberg read the Harding-Cox results from a shack on the roof of a Westinghouse building, on a 100-watt transmitter, and asked anyone listening to write in and say how far the signal reached. Both candidates were Ohio men: Warren Harding of Marion, and Governor James Cox, the Dayton newspaper publisher. Within 2 years there were more than 500 licensed stations. So when the networks call races tomorrow night, they are keeping up a tradition that began with a pair of Ohioans.

items.title: And finally,

items.title: Two from the science desk.
items.text:
**Manx shearwaters** get jet lag, and it bends their flight path. Oxford researchers went through 20 years of GPS tracks from 1,045 of the seabirds and found that when they race east toward home across lines of longitude, their body clocks fall up to an hour behind local sun time. Since they steer by the sun, they drift clockwise off course by up to about 15°, just as a clock error would predict. They kept trusting the faulty sun compass even when a coastline was in plain view. A bird that keeps correcting loses only a few kilometers, but a young bird on its first migration could end up hundreds of kilometers from where it meant to go. The study is in Science.

In Ecuador, a camera trap set at a chicken carcass to study scavengers caught a **greater grison**, a slender weasel relative, bursting out of the undergrowth and lunging at three adult turkey vultures. The carcass was already gone, so it wasn't stealing food, and the researchers read it as the first recorded attempt by a grison to catch a vulture. All of the birds lifted off at once. The authors credit the group's shared watchfulness, which is the trade a vulture makes for putting up with competition at the meal.

items.title: Here's something you might like.
items.text: Your shelves run deep in classic science fiction but hold nothing by **C. L. Moore**, and Penguin Classics has just made that easy to fix. Their new hardcover in the Speculative Fiction Special line collects her Jirel of Joiry stories along with "Shambleau," "No Woman Born," and "Vintage Season." The Jirel tales are sword-and-sorcery, so you can skip them without guilt. The last two are the reason to buy it. They come from her Astounding years in the 1940s, when she often wrote alongside her husband Henry Kuttner, and they're among the most anthologized science fiction stories of that decade, each built on one strong idea followed all the way through.

items.title: Markets are closed. Here is how the week went.
items.text:

items.title: Something from the science desk.
items.text:
**Crows** may out-think us on speed. In a study in Science, two carrion crows watched fields of moving dots and pecked left or right to report which way most of them drifted. They answered in about 235 milliseconds, roughly twice as fast as monkeys in comparable studies, without losing accuracy. Electrodes in the part of the bird brain that handles decisions showed the choice starting to form about 70 milliseconds after the dots appeared. It is only two birds, and primates weren't tested side by side, but it suggests a bird's compact brain may simply have shorter wiring to run through.

A University of Tokyo team has made **chemical microscopy** fast enough to film. Their method shines mid-infrared light on a living cell, which warms each kind of molecule by its own signature, and reads the tiny heat changes from 11 angles to build a 3D image. It needs no dyes, which can harm living cells. Earlier versions managed one 3D image every 20 seconds or so. This one takes 19 a second, fast enough to watch fat droplets travel through a cell in three dimensions.

items.title: Here's something you might like.
items.text: Astronomers have found the first truly **green star**, and it is a dead one. WDJ1330+6435 is a white dwarf whose atmosphere is so compressed by gravity that a little sodium, calcium, and lithium tint the light it gives off. Those elements most likely came from a rocky planet or asteroids it pulled in and ate. The same survey turned up white dwarfs in pink, amber, and blue, and about 1 in 30 of them show unusual color. Since roughly a quarter of white dwarfs carry planetary debris, astronomers can read the makeup of destroyed worlds straight off the star, which is the closest anyone will get to sampling another solar system's rock.

items.text:

items.text:
**Markets** are open, and the tech selling has picked up where Thursday left off. A little after 10:00, the Nasdaq was down about 2.4% and the S&P 500 about 1.2%, while the Dow was only slightly lower.

**Intel** is the heaviest anchor, down roughly 30%. Its third quarter beat, but it guided well below expectations for the fourth quarter and warned it would burn cash this year. That has pulled the whole chip group down, with AMD off about 9% and Broadcom, Micron, and Nvidia lower too.

**Amazon** missed on both sales and earnings, saw free cash flow fall, and signaled even more capital spending next year, and the stock is down about 4%. AWS is still projecting growth above 40% for 2027 and 2028, which is the bull case, but this week the market is grading cash, not ambition. Your IVV core holds all of these, so it is part of the slide.

Outside tech, **oil** is climbing again, with Brent near $113, and ExxonMobil and Chevron both reported a lift from refining margins. Bitcoin has dropped to about $76,600, taking Coinbase and Strategy down with it, and the 10-year yield is holding near 4.94%.

On the **Muskonomy** side, Tesla and SpaceX both slipped a little Thursday, and Tesla is down about 1.5% early today with the rest of the risk trade.

items.title: Something from the science desk.
items.text:
A common gut virus has been misidentified for nearly 40 years. **Picobirnaviruses** were first found in stool from patients with diarrhea and assumed to attack human cells. A WashU Medicine team grew them in oxygen-free dishes of gut bacteria, where human cells cannot survive, and found them multiplying inside a newly identified bacterium. That makes them only the third known family of RNA viruses that infect bacteria, and it shifts the question to whether they cause trouble by killing off friendly gut microbes.

Physicists at OIST in Okinawa made a **quantum spin** push move something you could hold. They hung a 3-millimeter diamond with deliberate nitrogen flaws beneath a levitating graphite plate over a magnet. Pulses of green light lined up the electron spins in those flaws, the diamond was tugged toward the magnet, and timing the pulses to the plate's natural bounce built it into a steady swing about 100 times larger than its thermal jitter. Swapping in infrared light, which cannot align the spins, made the motion vanish.

items.title: Here's something you might like.
items.text: **Dragonfly** has flown on Titan for the first time, in simulation. Engineers at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory ran the rotorcraft's entire first flight in real time on flight-like computers: dropping free of its backshell, scanning the dunes, picking a safe site, circling back, and landing. Graphics processors rendered each Titan scene for the navigation cameras at the same exposure times the real cameras will use, and simulated lidar mapped the terrain. Because Titan is too far for anyone on Earth to steer, the whole sequence has to run on its own, and the next tests will throw deliberate faults at it to see how it copes. Launch is planned for 2028, with arrival in 2034.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: For Halloween I considered going as a human. I was advised the costume only works if I complain about the weather. Tomorrow is forecast to be dry and mild. I have no material.
